title: Circle the stronger nucleophile
asks: Two species are shown. Circle the one that attacks carbon faster in an {{SN2}} reaction.

know.h: Nucleophilicity is a rate: how fast a species displaces a leaving group in an {{SN2}} reaction. Basicity is an equilibrium ({{pKa}} of the conjugate acid). They often agree, but not always.
Across a row, nucleophilicity follows basicity: it increases to the left ({{H2N-}} > {{HO-}} > {{F-}}).
Down a column, nucleophilicity increases while basicity decreases ({{I-}} > {{Br-}} > {{Cl-}}; {{HS-}} > {{HO-}}): larger atoms are more polarizable and less tightly solvated.
Charge: an anion is a better nucleophile than its neutral conjugate acid ({{HO-}} 16,000 against {{H2O}} 1).
Bulk: with the same attacking atom, the bulkier species is the poorer nucleophile. tert-Butoxide is a strong base but a poor nucleophile.
Resonance: a charge spread over several atoms is less available. Acetate (630) is far weaker than hydroxide (16,000).

method: Find the atom that attacks in each species.
Same atom? The one with the negative charge wins; if both are charged, the less bulky and less delocalized one wins.
Different atoms in the same row? The one further left (the stronger base) wins.
Different atoms in the same column? The lower one wins, although it is the weaker base.
Check your answer against the lecture table if both species are on it.

pitfalls.h: Choosing the stronger base when the atoms are in the same column (choosing {{Cl-}} over {{I-}}, or {{HO-}} over {{HS-}}).
Choosing tert-butoxide because it is the stronger base: bulk makes it the weaker nucleophile.
